title: How caches work
objectives: Predict cache misses from an access pattern and a line size.

screens.title: Which reads miss
screens.prose: From the C++ pricing course: memory moves in 64-byte lines, 8 doubles each. Here each row is one line. The cache starts empty, and a loop adds `a[0]` to `a[31]` in order.

state.caption: Each row of 8 doubles is one 64-byte line.

screens.question: Tap every access that misses.

hints.text: A miss loads the whole line around the double it wanted.
The read of `a[0]` brings in `a[1]` to `a[7]`.
The first read of each row misses: indices 0, 8, 16 and 24.

feedback.correct: Four misses and 28 hits: a hit rate of 87.5%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Only the first read of each line misses.

byKey.c1: `a[1]` shares a line with `a[0]`, so the first miss already brought it in.
byKey.c8: `a[8]` starts a new line, so its read misses.
byKey.c32: The loop stops at `a[31]`; `a[32]` is never read.
byKey.c7: `a[7]` is the last double of the first line, loaded with `a[0]`.

explain.text: Each miss loads a whole 64-byte line, so 4 misses serve 32 reads. That is 28 hits, a hit rate of 87.5%. Today we ask what happens when the cache is full.

screens.title: Five lines, four slots
screens.prose: A small cache holds 4 lines. When it is full, a miss throws out the line used least recently. Sweeping 32 doubles (4 lines) three times misses only 4 times. Now the loop sweeps 40 doubles: 5 lines, three times.

state.caption: The cache is empty. Move the slider to fetch the first line.

screens.question: Step through the fetches. How many of the 120 reads miss?

widget.accept: 15: every one of the 15 line fetches misses.

hints.text: Watch which line each miss throws out.
Line 4 throws out line 0, which the next sweep needs first.
Every fetch misses: 5 lines times 3 sweeps.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Step through all 15 line fetches and read the count.

byKey.five: 5 is the first sweep alone. The second sweep misses on every line too.
byKey.cold: You counted 5 cold misses and one eviction. Each miss evicts the line needed next.
byKey.each: Only the first double of each line can miss; the other 7 hit.

explain.text: Each miss evicts the least recently used line, which is the one the loop needs next. So all 15 line fetches miss. We call this rule **least recently used** (LRU) eviction.

screens.title: Two arrays, one set
screens.prose: Arrays `a` and `b` start 256 bytes apart. A loop reads `a[i]` then `b[i]` for i = 0 to 7: 16 reads. The cache has 4 lines, grouped into sets of w **ways**. Line L may only go in set L mod (4 / w).

state.caption: One way, gap 256: line 0 of a and line 4 of b both map to set 0.

screens.question: Fill in the misses and the hit rate.

hints.text: Find the line of `a[0]` and of `b[0]`.
`a` is line 0 and `b` is line 4. With one way there are 4 sets.
One way: both in set 0, 16 misses. Two ways: both fit, 2 misses. Gap 320: line 5, set 1, 2 misses.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out each array's line and set first.

byKey.r0c2: With one way, lines 0 and 4 both need set 0, so each read throws out the other array.
byKey.r1c2: Two ways give set 0 room for both lines: only the two first touches miss.
byKey.r2c2: A gap of 320 puts `b` in line 5, which is set 1. No clash.
byKey.r0c3: No read hits when every read evicts the line the next read needs.

explain.text: With one way, line 0 and line 4 fight over set 0, so all 16 reads miss: a **conflict miss**. Two ways, or a gap of 320 bytes, gives each line a place: 2 misses, 87.5% hits.

canvas.caption: Gap 320: a in set 0, b in set 1.

screens.title: Sets and ways
screens.prose: A cache of 8 lines reads lines 0, 4, 8, 0. Spread the 8 lines as w ways in 8 / w sets.

state.caption: One way: lines 0 and 8 share set 0; line 4 has set 4.

screens.question: Fill in the sets and the misses for each number of ways.

hints.text: Lines 0, 4 and 8 share a set whenever the set count divides 4.
With 2 ways and 4 sets, lines 0, 4 and 8 all need set 0.
1 way: 4. 2 ways: 4. 4 ways: 3. 8 ways: 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each row, find the set of lines 0, 4 and 8.

byKey.r1c2: Two ways in set 0 hold lines 0 and 4. Line 8 then throws out line 0.
byKey.r0c2: With 8 sets, lines 0 and 8 share set 0, so line 8 evicts line 0.
byKey.r2c2: Four ways hold lines 0, 4 and 8 together, so the second read of line 0 hits.

explain.text: Lines 0, 4 and 8 crowd into one set until a set has room for three. With 4 or 8 ways it does, and line 0 hits. More ways means fewer conflict misses.

screens.title: Four of five
screens.prose: The 4-line LRU cache again. A loop sweeps the same 5 lines over and over.

state.caption: After sweep 1: lines 1 to 4 are held. The loop now wants line 0.

screens.question: How many line fetches in the second sweep hit?

options.text: 4: four of the five lines are still held
options.why: You kept four of the five lines, but each miss evicts the line the loop needs next.
Line 0 misses first, and that miss pushes out line 1, the next one needed.
That needs room for five lines. The cache holds four.

hints.text: Which line does the loop want first, and is it held?
Line 0 is gone. Fetching it throws out line 1.
Each miss evicts the next line wanted, so nothing hits.

feedback.correct: None. Every fetch of the second sweep misses.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the evictions line by line.

byKey.b: Four lines are held, but always the wrong four. Each miss throws out the line needed next.
byKey.c: Fetching line 0 evicts line 1, then fetching line 1 evicts line 2, and so on.

explain.text: Line 0 misses and evicts line 1; line 1 misses and evicts line 2, all the way round. A loop one line bigger than an LRU cache hits nothing.

screens.title: When order does not matter
screens.prose: A 64 × 64 matrix of doubles is 32 KiB: exactly the size of this L1 cache. Both loop orders read all 4,096 doubles once.
screens.question: How many misses does the column-by-column walk make?

widget.accept: 512: one per line, because every line stays.

hints.text: Does the whole matrix fit?
32 KiB is 512 lines, and the cache holds 512.
Each line misses once and then stays.

feedback.correct: 512, the same as row by row.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether a line can be evicted at all.

byKey.all: 4,096 misses would need every line to leave before its next use. Here nothing is evicted.
byKey.rows: 64 is the number of rows. The matrix spans 512 lines.

explain.text: The matrix fills the 64 sets exactly, 8 lines in each, so no line is ever evicted. Both orders miss 512 times. Order matters only when the data does not fit.

screens.title: Two rules
screens.prose:
Every count today came from two rules:

$$\text{line} = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{address}}{64} \right\rfloor, \qquad \text{set} = \text{line} \bmod \frac{n}{w}$$

Here n is lines and w is ways. A read misses on a line's first touch, and again if its set evicted it since.
screens.question: A cache of 512 lines with 8 ways. Which set holds byte address 4,160?

options.why: 65 is the line number. Take it mod 64 sets.
You divided the address by the 512 lines.
Line 64 is in set 0, but address 4,160 is in line 65.

hints.text: Find the line first.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide by 64 for the line, then take it mod the sets.

explain.text: $4{,}160 / 64 = 65$, and there are $512 / 8 = 64$ sets, so set 1. Lines that are 64 apart share a set.

screens.title: Drill: misses
screens.prose: Drill: about 90 seconds each. Say the reasoning aloud first. Cache sizes and costs here are round figures: know them to a power of ten. A cold cache is empty at the start and large enough unless stated.
screens.question: Fill in the misses.

hints.text: A stride under 8 still touches every line.
64 doubles are 8 lines and 96 doubles are 12.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Stride 4 reads two doubles per line, so 8 lines, 8 misses.
byKey.r1c1: 96 doubles are 12 lines, and stride 3 touches each.
byKey.r2c1: Each miss evicts the line needed next: 5 times 3.
byKey.r3c1: Four lines fit, so only the first sweep misses.
byKey.r4c1: Lines 0, 4 and 8 share set 0, which holds two.
byKey.r5c1: Set 0 holds four lines, so the second read of line 0 hits.

explain.text: A stride below 8 doubles touches every line once. A loop that fits misses only on first touch. A loop one line too big misses on every fetch.

screens.title: Follow-up: a lattice by column
screens.prose: The interviewer asks why a lattice stored row by row is slow when walked by column. Take a 1,000 × 1,000 matrix of doubles, the 32 KiB L1 cache, and 100 ns a miss.

state.caption: Each number is a place in memory. Rows are contiguous; a column jumps a whole row.

screens.question: Fill in the misses and the time for each loop order.

hints.text: By rows, each line serves 8 reads.
By columns, consecutive reads are 8,000 bytes apart, and a column spans 1,000 lines.

feedback.correct: 125,000 misses in 12.5 ms, against 1,000,000 in 100 ms.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the reads each line serves in each order.

byKey.r0c1: A million doubles at 8 a line is 125,000 lines.
byKey.r1c1: A column touches 1,000 lines, more than the 512 the cache holds, so every read misses.

explain.text: By rows, 125,000 misses take 12.5 ms; by columns, all 1,000,000 miss and take 100 ms. At 64 × 64 the matrix fits and both orders cost the same. In a pricer, put the contiguous index in the inner loop.

ideas: Memory moves in 64-byte lines; a read whose line is cached hits, otherwise it misses and loads the line.
Line L lives in set L mod (n / w), so lines a set apart can evict each other.
A loop one line bigger than an LRU cache misses on every fetch; data that fits misses only once.

formula.name: Where a line lives
formula.note: n lines in total, w ways per set.

summary.trap: Thinking four of five lines still help: under LRU each miss evicts the line needed next.

quiz.prose: An `int` is 4 bytes. A loop reads 64 ints in order from a cold cache.
quiz.question: How many reads miss?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count bytes, then lines.

byKey.each: Only the first int of each line misses.
byKey.doubles: 8 misses would be 64 doubles. An int is half the size.
byKey.perline: 16 is the number of ints in one line.

explain.text: 64 ints are 256 bytes, which is 4 lines of 64. Each line misses once.

quiz.prose: A cache of 16 lines with 4 ways.
quiz.question: Which set holds byte address 448?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the line, then take it mod the number of sets.

byKey.line: 7 is the line, and would be the set with 16 sets. There are 16 / 4 = 4 sets.
byKey.quotient: You took $7 \div 4 = 1$, the quotient. The set is the remainder, $7 \bmod 4 = 3$.

quiz.prose: In a direct-mapped cache, arrays `a` and `b` keep throwing each other out.
quiz.question: Which change stops it?

options.why: Swapping the reads does not change which set each line uses.
Smaller elements shift nothing: both arrays still start in the same set.
A second read of a line that was just evicted misses again.

feedback.correct: Moving `b` one line puts it in the next set.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What decides which set a line uses?

explain.text: The set is the line number mod the number of sets. Shifting `b` by 64 bytes moves it to the next set, so the clash ends.

quiz.prose: A 4-line LRU cache. A loop sweeps 3 lines four times.
quiz.question: How many line fetches miss?

widget.accept: 3: the lines fit, so only first touches miss.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Do 3 lines fit in 4?

byKey.all: 12 would need each line evicted between uses. Three lines fit in four.
byKey.one: Each of the 3 lines misses on its first touch.

explain.text: Three lines fit in four slots, so only the three first touches miss. The other 9 fetches hit.
